newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian PM defends monarchy, royalist politics.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian PM defends monarchy, royalist politics.

text.p: Cambodian Co-Premier Prince Norodom Ranariddh on Tuesday defended the country's monarchy and warned that any attempt to force royalist politicians to resign would amount to a coup d'etat.

"It is not fair to ask the royal family to resign from a life of royalism before entering politics. When has the royal family done something wrong? When has the royal family been national traitors in the Kingdom of Cambodia?...

"If this country is made into a republic, it means we have had a coup d'etat," Ranariddh said in an angry speech at a school opening in northwestern Cambodia. "This is a coup d'etat by category because they want us (the royalists) to resign."

The prince underlined the virtues of the constitutional monarchy and emphasised that royalty had suffered along with most of the rest of the population in the past quarter century of turmoil, including the disastrous "Killing Fields" reign of the Khmer Rouge from 1975 to early 1979.
He said they were entitled to the same rights as other citizens.

The comments stepped up the rhetoric in a heated exchange between Ranariddh and co-Premier Hun Sen, who at the weekend said he would ask King Norodom Sihanouk, Ranariddh's father, to ban members of the royal family from politics unless they renounced their royal positions.
Tensions between Ranarridh and Hun Sen have flared repeatedly over the past year, widening rifts in the fractured coalition government they formed following polls in 1993.
Ranariddh's royalist FUNCINPEC party and Hun Sen's ex-communist Cambodian People's Party are preparing to run against each other in local and national elections scheduled for 1997 and 1998.
Tuesday was the eve of a FUNCINPEC congress expected to take up election issues. The FUNCINPEC party issued a point-by-point statement on Tuesday attacking Hun Sen's recent remarks.

Hun Sen, apparently made uneasy by remarks by Sihanouk that he was considering abdication, has spoken out against royalist politicians in recent days and warned he would cancel the coming elections if the king re-entered politics.
The immensely popular Sihanouk abdicated to enter politics in 1955 after 14 years on the throne.
In an apparent reaction to the attacks, Ranariddh said, "Social security and peace are being threatened."
He appealed to Hun Sen's party and others to sign an agreement to respect the constitution and said he remained determined to hold local and national elections on schedule in 1997 and 1998.
Ranariddh has said Hun Sen's threats to delay elections if Sihanouk abdicated would violate the constitution -- a position backed by his ally Khmer Nation Party president, Sam Rainsy.
